body.heading: Rays from a dark mineral
paragraphs: In 1896, Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts fogged photographic plates even in darkness — they were emitting invisible rays. Marie Curie, a Polish-born physicist working in Paris, took up the puzzle with her husband Pierre, measuring the rays precisely and showing they came from the uranium atoms themselves.

She coined the word radioactivity for the phenomenon. Testing every known element, she found thorium also emitted rays — and that a uranium ore called pitchblende was far more radioactive than its uranium could explain. Something unknown and much stronger was hiding inside it.

body.heading: Tonnes of ore, grams of discovery
paragraphs: The Curies' laboratory was a leaky shed. There, over four years, they processed tonnes of pitchblende residue — stirring boiling vats by hand — slowly concentrating the hidden elements. In 1898 they announced two new ones: polonium, named for Marie's occupied homeland, and radium, which glowed faintly in the dark and warmed itself.

Marie Curie went on to win two Nobel Prizes, in physics and in chemistry — still the only person to win in two different sciences. During the First World War she organised mobile X-ray units, driven to the front to help surgeons find shrapnel in wounded soldiers.

body.heading: The price, and the lesson
paragraphs: Nobody then understood the danger. The Curies handled radioactive material daily, carried it in pockets, and marvelled at its glow; Marie died in 1934 of an illness almost certainly caused by her years of exposure. Her notebooks remain radioactive today and are kept in lead-lined boxes.

Modern science kept her discoveries and learned her lesson: protective shielding, distance and monitoring now guard everyone who works with radiation, and radium's medical descendants treat cancers with precision she would have admired.

takeaway: Marie Curie's patient chemistry revealed polonium and radium and founded radioactivity science — at a personal cost that taught science to protect its own.
